questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Derivative of a Parametric Curve
questions.problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x={e}^{2t},\,y=({t}^{2}-1){e}^{-t},\,-\infty <t<\infty ,
$$

 find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $P$ on the curve where $t=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2{e}^{2t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=(1+2t-{t}^{2}){e}^{-t}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{(1+2t-{t}^{2}){e}^{-t}}{2{e}^{2t}}=\frac{1}{2}(1+2t-{t}^{2}){e}^{-3t}.
$$

At the point where $t=1$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{1}{2}(1+2(1)-(1)^{2}){e}^{-3(1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1+2-1){e}^{-3} \\  & ={e}^{-3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=2\sqrt{t},\,y=12t+1,\,0\le t<\infty ,
$$

 find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $P$ on the curve where $t=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},\,{y}^{′}(t)=12.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{12}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}}=12\sqrt{t}.
$$

At the point where $t=1$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =12\sqrt{1} \\  & =12\,.\end{aligned}
$$

For the parametric curve (shown above)

$$
x=3{t}^{2}-2t,\,y={t}^{2}-1,\,-\infty <t<\infty ,
$$

 find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $P$ on the curve where $t=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=6t-2,\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2t}{6t-2}=\frac{t}{3t-1}.
$$

At the point where $t=2$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{2}{3(2)-1} \\  & =\frac{2}{6-1} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=12\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,y=15\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi ,
$$

 calculate $\frac{dy}{dx}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=12\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=-15\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-15\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{12\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }=-\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .
$$

For the parametric curve (shown above)

$$
x=5\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,y=\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,0\le t<2\pi ,
$$

find the derivative $\frac{dy}{dx}$ at the point $P$ on the curve where $t=\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Do not round the answer.

$\frac{dy}{dx}{|}_{t\,=\,\pi /6}=$ 
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=10\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=-2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{(-2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)}{10\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{5}\operatorname{tan}⁡2t.
$$

At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{5}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{5}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{5}\cdot \sqrt{3} \\  & =-\frac{3}{5}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Slope of the Tangent to a Parametric Curve at a Given Point
questions.problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},\,y=\frac{{e}^{t}}{2t},\,-\infty <t<\infty ,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=5.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-\frac{1}{4}{t}^{-3/2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=\frac{2t{e}^{t}-2{e}^{t}}{4{t}^{2}}=\frac{{e}^{t}(t-1)}{2{t}^{2}}.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{e}^{t}(t-1)}{2{t}^{2}}\cdot (-4{t}^{3/2}) \\  & =-\frac{2{e}^{t}(t-1)}{\sqrt{t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=5,$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =-\,\frac{2{e}^{5}(5-1)}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =-\,\frac{2{e}^{5}\cdot 4}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =-\,\frac{8{e}^{5}}{\sqrt{5}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

For the parametric curve 

$$
x={t}^{3}+2{t}^{2},\,y={t}^{2},\,-\infty <t<\infty ,
$$

shown above, calculate the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=2.$ Do not round the answer.

$m=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}+4t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t.
$$

 

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{2t}{3{t}^{2}+4t} \\  & =\frac{2}{3t+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=2,$ the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{dy}{dx}\,{|}_{t\,=\,2} & =\frac{2}{3(2)+4} \\  & =\frac{2}{6+4} \\  & =\frac{2}{10} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,y={sin}^{2}⁡t,\,0\le t<2\pi ,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{12}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t=\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=\frac{\pi }{12},$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{12}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y=t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,0\le t<2\pi ,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=1-\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})} \\  & =\frac{1-1}{1+0} \\  & =0\,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x={e}^{1/t},\,y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}-1}},\,1<t<\infty ,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}{e}^{1/t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=-\frac{t}{({t}^{2}-1)^{3/2}}.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{(-\frac{t}{({t}^{2}-1)^{3/2}})}{(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}{e}^{1/t})} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{3}{e}^{-1/t}}{({t}^{2}-1)^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=2,$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{2}^{3}{e}^{-1/2}}{({2}^{2}-1)^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{8}{{3}^{3/2}\sqrt{e}} \\  & =\frac{8}{\sqrt{27e}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=\cos{t}, \quad y=\sin{t}, \qquad  0\leq t<2\pi,
$$

 calculate $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13949328/assets/2ec95dd061fa6b7f09c9f899a1f6483b4ea7d5127372ddd6eefb74d6ed10c14c.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
x'(t) = -\sin{t}, \qquad y'(t)=\cos{t}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\cos t}{-\sin t} = -\cot t.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=te^t, \quad y=e^{-t}, \qquad -\infty < t <\infty,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=1.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
x'(t) = e^t + te^t = (1+t)e^t, \qquad y'(t)=-e^{-t}.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{-{e}^{-t}}{(1+t){e}^{t}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{(1+t){e}^{2t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =-\frac{1}{{e}^{2(1)}(1+1)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$
